To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the three-phase respiratory pattern can transform into two-phase and one-phase oscillations through intermediate regimes and that the persistent sodium current contributes to the control of respiratory rhythm generation and transitions between functional states.

the three-, two- and one-phase respiratory oscillatory patterns observed in brain stem slices can be produced by a simple neural circuit composed of mutually inhibitory and excitatory neurons, and that the transitions between these patterns can be explained by the dynamics of the same neural circuit.

the three-phase respiratory pattern, which is observed during normal breathing, changes with alterations in physiological conditions and that a minimal neural network proposed in our recent study can reproduce these transformations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms underlying the generation of the rhythmic respiratory pattern and its control by the central pattern generator.
the generation of respiratory rhythm and pattern in the mammalian brain stem.
the mechanisms of respiratory rhythm generation in the mammalian brain stem and how these mechanisms are altered during pathological conditions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the model presented in the article by Rybak et al. (2010) provides a plausible mechanism for the generation of the respiratory rhythm and its phase transitions.

I(NaP), although not required for the generation of respiratory rhythm, contributes to the generation of respiratory rhythms and their transitions between different states, and thus is an important component for the respiratory central pattern generation.
the model is able to capture all of the major features of the experimental data and that the mechanisms of state transitions can be explained in terms of the model.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a minimal neural circuit composed of mutually inhibitory postinspiratory and expiratory neurons and a single preinspiratory cell with persistent sodium current-dependent intrinsic burst activity is sufficient to reproduce the three-, two- and one-phase oscillations observed in in situ perfused brain stem preparations.

the three-phase pattern is generated by the interaction of a ring of three mutually inhibitory neurons with a preinspiratory burst generator, which dynamically participates in the phase transitions between expiratory and inspiratory phases and controls the duration of the inspiratory phase.
the respiratory network is able to switch between multiple rhythmic states and that these changes can be induced by changes in the synaptic drives to the network.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the three-phase respiratory rhythm is not the only rhythm that can be generated in the respiratory central pattern generating network.

the three-, two- and one-phase oscillations in the network can all be produced without I(NaP), but the network with I(NaP)-dependent neurons is more robust and can generate a broader range of oscillatory regimes.

, in the model, a single neuron with intrinsic bursting properties can be responsible for the transitions between the respiratory states, and the transition between states can be mediated through the transitions between respiratory phases within the same state.
